kevin: Pushed a short perf dump from today's canary. p95 host-side latency jumped ~18% after the kernel-selector change. Attaching profiler snippet and a quick note on where I think the overhead is (tokenization + parsing + chunk framing).

maya: ugh. do you have flamegraphs?

kevin: Yep — pasted key stacks below. This is a 4s sample around a spike handling streaming chat messages (grpc). Noticed a lot more time in our request parser and io_fracture (stream framing).

kevin: ```
# top stacks (abridged)
- grpc::StreamRead -> request_parser::parse_chunks -> tokenization::encode -> kernel_selector::choose -> runtime::dispatch
- http::Parse -> chunker::fragment -> tokenization::encode -> runtime::dispatch

p95_host_before: 72ms
p95_host_after: 85ms
median_host_before: 12ms
median_host_after: 14ms
```

jonah: hmm. kernel_selector change was supposed to be a cheap check. could it be forcing a hot path that invalidates our fast-path in tokenization?

olivia: I remember a similar regression where an extra header check forced us into the fallback parser. Are we doing any new header parsing for compat?

kevin: We do now probe for "x-rd-model-variant" earlier to decide micro-batching. That probe is a tiny memcmp, but the probe also triggers a codepath that touches more of the request struct which prevents the fast inlining in parse_token_batch. The profiler shows inline boundary break.

maya: can you show the minimal repro? even a short curl + stream that trips it would help.

kevin: Minimal repro gist: client opens grpc stream and sends 3 small bursts (10 tokens each) with model header toggled. When header present, stream-fragmenter chooses fragmentation mode B which adds an extra framing pass. With header absent, mode A uses prefix-merge and avoids the extra copy.

kevin: ```
# repro (pseudo)
client: open stream -> send(header: x-rd-model-variant: v2) -> send(payload 10 tokens) x3
server: chunker.fragment(mode=B) -> parser.deserialize_batches -> tokenizer.encode -> dispatch
```

ai-perf-bot: Quick note: KV-cache hit rate unchanged (98%). Not the culprit.

jonah: if KV cache is fine then it's purely host preproc. Two levers: avoid the extra framing copy or rework kernel_selector to not probe until after parsing. Which is less risky?

olivia: Reordering the probe seems safer: parse first, then pick kernel based on parsed metadata. That avoids touching parse hot-paths. But it may delay batching decisions by ~0.4ms which might affect throughput.

maya: Could we do a cheap hint instead of full probe? e.g., read the header position via offset table without decoding?

kevin: Tried a hint: read 1 byte to check presence -> still caused same inline boundary because we call header_accessor() which is virtual. The problem is side-effectful calls into request metadata path.

kevin: Another datapoint: switching to HTTP/2 framing reduced overhead compared to raw framed grpc for small bursts because the HTTP/2 flow merges tiny frames. But we can't flip protocol. Worth noting for dedicated customers traffic shaping.

jonah: Any numbers for streaming chunk size distributions? Maybe our batching heuristics assume larger chunks and then we pay cost for many tiny chunks.

kevin: Sampled 10k streams: 64% have mean chunk <= 12 tokens, 22% in [13..48], rest >48. So many small-fragment streams. Our batching heuristics tune for median=32 which is off for these chat flows.

olivia: Proposed action items: 1) revert kernel_selector early probe (hotfix) 2) add a fast non-virtual header peek API 3) tweak batching heuristics to bias small-chunk streams 4) add lightweight telemetry: measure per-stream chunk count and time spent in framing vs tokenization.

maya: +1 on telemetry. Also add a canary that forces mode=B so we can measure end-to-end impact before/after changes.

kevin: I'll open a PR with the revert + unit to prove no functional change. Putting a benchmark that simulates 10000 tiny bursts.

ai-perf-bot: Benchmark suggestion: run with kernels: {fp16-vec, int8-vec} and kernel_selector: early_probe vs post-parse. Measure p50/p95 host and device.

kevin: quick ci-local run results (simulated):
```
scenario A (early_probe): p95_host=87ms, p50_host=15ms
scenario B (post-parse): p95_host=73ms, p50_host=14ms
device token throughput ~ unchanged
```

jonah: That delta matches production. Reverting early_probe seems low-risk and high-reward.

olivia: For the long term, we should: - make fragmentation zero-copy for mode B (merge buffers) - adjust heuristics so small-chunk streams get aggregated aggressively - add landing pages in runtime to summarize host vs device breakdown per route

maya: Also file an ENG-RUN ticket for SLO impact and timeline. Ops needs to know if we plan a rollback.

kevin: Opening PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4521 (WIP). Will attach flamegraph + tracer spans.

sre-bot: Notifying oncall: @oncall-runtime. Potential regression impacting hosted streaming.

jonah: Thanks. I'll review PR and help with the canary plan.

kevin: tl;dr: regression introduced by early kernel selector probe that touches parse hot path -> increases copies/framing -> p95 up ~18%. Hotfix: revert probe, add non-virtual peek, and follow-up batching tweaks.

maya: cool. keep updates here. :thumbsup:
